source: Shepard & Metzler (1971) Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects, Science 171:701-703
finding: People judged whether two 3D block figures were the same shape. Reaction time rose in a straight line with the angle between the two figures. Same slope for rotation in the picture plane and in depth.
numbers: Linear RT-by-angle function, roughly 1 s near 0 deg to roughly 4-5 s near 180 deg, about 60 deg/s (recalled from memory, not read this session; small N of about 8 observers)
limits: Paper itself not opened (paywalled). Wikipedia (a03) confirms only the linear RT claim. Niall (2020, 2023) argues depth effects may come from flat-picture properties.
agent_relevance: The founding 'analog' result: cost grows with the amount of transformation. A symbolic solver would not show it. For O6 it marks which tasks are naturally spatial.

source: Kosslyn, Ball & Reiser (1978) Visual images preserve metric spatial information (island map scanning)
finding: People memorised a fictional island map with 7 landmarks, then imagined a dot moving from one landmark to another. Scan time grew linearly with the real map distance.
numbers: 21 landmark pairs; RT-by-distance correlation reported very high (about r=.97, recalled from memory, not read this session)
limits: Not opened; numbers from memory. Pylyshyn (1981) and Intons-Peterson (1983) argue the linear time reflects what subjects think a scan should take (see a07, a08).
agent_relevance: Core evidence that images keep metric structure. For an LLM this is the argument for giving a spatial layout (grid, coordinates) instead of prose.

source: Wikipedia: Mental rotation
finding: Summarises Shepard-Metzler: reaction time linearly proportional to rotation angle. Parietal lobe, especially the intraparietal sulcus, is consistently active and activation grows with angle. Sex differences exist (Voyer 1995) but shrink with changed stimuli (Fisher 2017; Rahe 2021).
numbers: Harris et al. 2000 PET: 7 volunteers (4 male, 3 female), aged 29-66, activation in right posterior parietal lobe. Vandenberg & Kuse test: 20 items, angles 0/60/120/180 deg. No slopes given on the page.
quote: changing the stimuli can eliminate any male advantages
limits: Secondary source. No slope in ms per degree on the page.
agent_relevance: Shows the paradigm is robust enough to be a standard test (SpatialViz-type benchmarks reuse it) and that group effects depend on stimulus choice. Warn: benchmark results depend on item sets.

source: Wikipedia: Imagery debate
finding: Pictorialism (Kosslyn) holds that images are depictive, like a CRT display scanned by a mind's eye. Descriptivism (Pylyshyn) holds that mental representations are propositional, tree-structured, compositional, productive and systematic. Pylyshyn argued the burden is on pictorialists. Cooper & Shepard (1973): RT rises with rotation angle up to 180 deg and falls back by 360 deg.
numbers: Pearson & Kosslyn (2015) fMRI: viewing scenes strongly activated occipital areas; imagining mainly engaged prefrontal and parietal regions with weaker, diffuse occipital activity. Reisberg, Pearson & Kosslyn (2003): researchers' own imagery vividness related to their theory side.
quote: The first claims ... a mental image is depictive; the second claims it is descriptive (paraphrase of the page)
limits: Short encyclopedia page; no island-map or tacit-knowledge numbers.
agent_relevance: Gives the two formats we choose between when we pick a representation for a problem: depictive grid versus propositional list.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Nanay 2021) Mental Imagery
finding: Places Kosslyn (1980) in the imagistic corner and Pylyshyn (1981) in the propositional corner. Many participants, including some original ones, have declared the debate dead. Reisberg (2003): people with less vivid imagery leaned propositional; vivid imagers leaned iconic. Defines imagery as representing without the appropriate immediate sensory input. Cites Perky (1910): imagery can be confused with perception. Aphantasia (Zeman 2015) = no reported conscious imagery, measured with the VVIQ.
numbers: No numerical results on the page (text read to character 100000 of 117134).
quote: the condition of not having (or at least not reporting) any conscious mental imagery
limits: Philosophy overview, no data. Last 17k characters (bibliography) not read.
agent_relevance: Individual differences in imagery shaped which side researchers took. A reminder that 'the right representation' may differ by solver, so test per task, not by theory.

source: Pylyshyn (2002) Mental imagery: In search of a theory, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 25:157-182
finding: Abstract only (full text paywalled). Pylyshyn separates effects of the cognitive architecture from effects of tacit knowledge about what would happen in a visual scene. He argues the depictive claim explains nothing unless read literally as brain geometry, and that the literal reading fails, partly because the evidence is cognitively penetrable. Shared mechanisms with vision tell little about format. Neuroscience does not favour a picture theory. The null hypothesis stays: imagery uses the same representations and processes as general reasoning, with content about how things would look.
numbers: None in abstract. Page lists 368 citations.
quote: the assumption of the spatial or depictive nature of images is only explanatory if taken literally
limits: Only the abstract was read. The body (tacit-knowledge studies, FINST, cognitive penetrability argument) is not opened.
agent_relevance: Key warning: if a result follows from what the solver believes, it says nothing about format. For our agent: test a spatial form against a matched text form at equal information, not against a weaker prompt.

source: Pylyshyn (1981) The imagery debate: Analogue media versus tacit knowledge, Psychological Review 88:16-45
finding: Scan-time and rotation effects are not properties of an analog medium. They come from subjects' tacit knowledge of how real objects behave and from their wish to act as if they were scanning. If the task says 'imagine', subjects reproduce the timing they expect.
numbers: Argument paper, no new data (as recalled; not opened).
limits: Not opened. Intons-Peterson (1983) and Denis & Kosslyn (1999) are the empirical tests of this claim.
agent_relevance: For LLMs: a model may 'simulate' a visualisation just from text priors about how scenes behave. Visualisation output is not proof of spatial computation (compare a13, a14).

source: Intons-Peterson (1983) Imagery paradigms: How vulnerable are they to experimenters' expectations? JEP:HPP 9:394-412
finding: Different experimenters told subjects different expected outcomes. Subjects' scanning and rotation-style imagery results shifted in the expected direction, so some imagery effects are sensitive to demand and expectation.
numbers: Several experiments; exact N and slopes not read (recalled from memory only).
limits: Not opened. Later work (Denis & Kosslyn 1999; Kosslyn, Thompson & Ganis 2006) argues that some effects, such as scanning with unexpected tasks, survive without demand.
agent_relevance: Supports G3 spirit: an effect that follows the stated expectation proves nothing. When a prompt tells the model what to see, check that results still hold with neutral wording.

source: Finke & Pinker (1982) Spontaneous imagery scanning in mental extrapolation, JEP:LMC 8:142-147
finding: Subjects saw a dot pattern, then an arrow, and judged whether the arrow pointed at a dot that had been there. Time rose with the distance from arrow to dot even though no scanning was requested.
numbers: Linear time-distance effect without instruction to scan (recalled; not read).
limits: Not opened. Used as the reply to the demand-characteristics criticism.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous, uninstructed spatial effects are the stronger kind of evidence that a spatial format is being used.

source: Finke, Pinker & Farah (1989) Reinterpreting visual patterns in mental imagery, Cognitive Science 13:51-78
finding: Subjects followed spoken instructions to build and transform an imagined figure (for example a D rotated 90 degrees left with a J attached below gives an umbrella) and then named it. Many could find new interpretations without drawing. Used as a test that images are not just verbal descriptions.
numbers: Original had 12 items; exact success rates not read (the 2025 LLM paper a22 describes the item type and says about the original 12 items).
limits: Not opened directly. Item type described via McCarty & Morales (a22).
agent_relevance: This is the classic task now used to test LLMs without pixels (a22). It tests whether a mental form can be reinterpreted.

source: Chambers & Reisberg (1985) Can mental images be ambiguous? JEP:HPP 11:317-328
finding: Subjects formed an image of an ambiguous drawing (duck-rabbit) and almost none could reverse it, though they could when they drew it from memory. Images seem to be interpreted, not pure pictures.
numbers: Roughly none of 15 reversed from imagery (recalled; not read).
limits: Not opened. Peterson et al. (1992) later got reversals with hints, so the result is bounded.
agent_relevance: Images carry a committed reading. Same for a model's first framing: re-reading a written trace is not the same as re-seeing it. Supports external drawn state (a sketchpad) over internal imagery.

source: Anderson (1978) Arguments concerning representations for mental imagery, Psychological Review 85:249-277
finding: Any result explained by a pictorial representation plus a process can be matched by a propositional representation plus a different process. Behaviour alone cannot fix the format.
numbers: Formal argument, no data (from memory).
limits: Not opened. Kosslyn replied that brain evidence can break the tie.
agent_relevance: Practical lesson: judge a representation by task payoff, not by theory. Fits G7: keep a form only if it wins at equal tokens.

source: Pearson, Naselaris, Holmes & Kosslyn (2015) Mental Imagery: Functional Mechanisms and Clinical Applications, Trends Cogn Sci
finding: Claims visual imagery is a depictive internal representation that works like a weak form of perception, and that the imagery debate is effectively ended. V1 activity patterns encode both perceived and imagined images. Early-visual-cortex studies split: many reported no activity above baseline, a slightly larger number reported it.
numbers: At least 20 studies (1993-2010) compared early visual activity in imagery with perception or rest. Binocular rivalry: the imagined pattern is more likely to dominate a later rivalry display, and the effect grows with longer imagery time. Voxel-wise decoding of mental images first applied in 2006 (blob stimuli).
limits: Advocate review from the Kosslyn camp. Pylyshyn (a06) disputes that shared mechanisms settle format. Activity in V1 is seen with simple blob stimuli; vividness differs across people.
agent_relevance: The depictive camp's best current case. It argues spatial detail is stored as image-like pattern. For our agent it suggests spatial problems may need a real spatial carrier, not a verbal list.

source: Bridge, Harrold, Holmes, Stokes, Kennard (2012) Vivid visual mental imagery in the absence of the primary visual cortex, J Neurol 259:1062-1070
finding: Patient SBR has near-complete cortical blindness from damage restricted to calcarine gray matter, yet shows vivid imagery behaviourally and in fMRI. His imagery activation looked like that of sighted controls, while his perceptual responses were greatly attenuated.
numbers: VVIQ (1 = extremely vivid, 5 = no image): controls mean 2.3 (SD 0.6), SBR 1.9. One patient plus sighted controls.
quote: SBR exhibits vivid visual mental imagery both behaviorally and when measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging
limits: Single case. Challenges the claim that V1 is required for imagery. Damaged V1 is not entirely absent, and the authors note task and technique variation.
agent_relevance: Imagery can run without the earliest visual stage. Weakens the strongest 'literal picture in V1' reading and supports a looser, functional depictive account.

source: Wimmer, Robinson, Doherty (2017) Are developments in mental scanning and mental rotation related? Br J Dev Psychol
finding: Restates the standard picture: in the island task adults and children show a linear time-distance relation, and adults with autism do too. Mental rotation also shows depictive properties. The study tests whether scanning and rotation develop together in 4- to 10-year-olds versus adults.
numbers: Age range 4-10 years plus adults (task design read; effect sizes not extracted this session).
limits: Intro read for the island-task summary; results section not mined.
agent_relevance: Both signature effects appear early in development, which supports a basic, low-cost spatial format in humans. It does not tell us whether a model needs one.

source: Kosslyn, Thompson & Ganis (2006) The Case for Mental Imagery, Oxford University Press
finding: Book-length reply to Pylyshyn. Argues from behaviour, PET/fMRI and TMS that imagery uses depictive, topographically organised cortex shared with vision. Includes the Kosslyn et al. 1995 PET result that imagery of small versus large letters shifts activity along V1.
numbers: Details recalled only; no figures read this session.
limits: Not opened. The SEP (a05) cites it for a 'roughly triangle-pattern' activation of direction-sensitive V1 neurons during visualisation.
agent_relevance: Source of the depictive-camp model: a visual buffer, an attention window and a mind's eye that reads patterns. A direct design analogy for a 'grid state plus a reader'.

source: Kosslyn (1980) Image and Mind; Kosslyn (1994) Image and Brain, Harvard / MIT Press
finding: Computational theory with a surface-matrix visual buffer (a CRT-like 2D array), long-term memory with propositional files, and processes that generate, inspect, rotate, zoom and scan the image. Image size, scan and rotation costs follow from the medium.
numbers: Model description; no numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Wikipedia (a04) describes the CRT metaphor. Pylyshyn argues the matrix is an assumption written into the model, not a result.
agent_relevance: A concrete architecture: propositional store plus a spatial working buffer. It matches a scaffold with text memory and a grid scratchpad.

source: Tye (1991) The Imagery Debate, MIT Press
finding: Philosophical mediation. Tye accepts that images are not unstructured pictures and argues for a middle view in which images are symbolic but their format is distinct, with a spatial array that represents by resemblance of parts and a rich interpretation. Rejects both a pure pictorialist and a pure descriptive account.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened; summary from memory. Wikipedia (a04) cites only Tye (1984) as an overview.
agent_relevance: Supports a hybrid scaffold: a spatial array that must be read by symbolic rules, rather than choosing one pure format.

source: Zeman, Dewar & Della Sala (2015) Lives without imagery - Congenital aphantasia, Cortex
finding: Case report of a man who lost imagery after a procedure and later work on congenital cases. People without imagery often still do imagery tasks.
numbers: Prevalence figure 1-4% is given in the 2025 LLM paper (a22), read this session. Original paper not opened.
limits: Not opened. Keogh & Pearson (2018) found aphantasics lacked sensory imagery in binocular rivalry priming yet could do some tasks.
agent_relevance: Humans solve many spatial tasks with no felt image, so a propositional route can work. Do not assume only imagery-like forms help.

source: Wu, Mao, Zhang, Xia, Dong, Cui, Wei (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in LLMs, NeurIPS 2024
finding: Visualization-of-Thought (VoT) asks an LLM to draw the state after each reasoning step as a text grid. GPT-4 with VoT beat GPT-4 with CoT and without visualization on natural-language navigation, visual navigation and polyomino tiling. VoT beat the GPT-4V multimodal model on these tasks.
numbers: VoT scores: route planning completing rate 40.77, success rate 14.72; next-step prediction 55.28; visual tiling 63.94; natural-language navigation 59.00 (vs 35.50 without visualization, +23.5; CoT about 54.00 per table reading, p<0.16). Two-sample z-test p<0.05 vs baselines in the other tasks.
quote: Visualize the state after each reasoning step.
limits: Table text extraction is partly scrambled, so CoT baselines for route planning are not quoted. Text-grid pictures only. Tasks are synthetic. A one-model-family study (GPT-4) plus smaller models in a21.
agent_relevance: Direct O6 evidence: a text-drawn spatial state helps at equal prompt cost. It is the closest current analogue to Kosslyn's visual buffer.

source: Wu et al. (2024) VoT, analysis and boundary conditions (same paper)
finding: Visualizations are often wrong, but a correct one helps. VoT helps larger models more. VoT lost to CoT on a ring-rotation task that reduces to modular arithmetic.
numbers: State visualization accuracy about 24-26%; compliance with spatial constraints about 51-52%; correct decisions in 65-77% of cases when the visualization was accurate. Ring task (size 12, 200 items): CoT 52.5% vs VoT 49.5%. LLAMA3-70B VoT beat CoT on all tasks except visual tiling; LLAMA3-8B and GPT-3.5 gains small or none (for example GPT-3.5 NL navigation CoT 9.00 vs VoT 16.50, LLAMA3-8B 15.50 vs 26.00). Removing the word 'reasoning' from the prompt raised tracking rate 78.5 points to 98.5%, final accuracy +3.5 to 62.5%.
limits: Low visualization accuracy means the spatial state is mostly unreliable; benefit depends on model size and on the prompt wording.
agent_relevance: Use a spatial form where a task has spatial state; use arithmetic where the task reduces to it. Check the drawn state with code (G2, G3) because most drawings are wrong.

source: McCarty & Morales (2025/2026) Artificial Phantasia: Emergent Mental Imagery in Large Language Models
finding: Extends the Finke, Pinker & Farah (1989) imagine-and-name task to dozens of new text items. The best reasoning LLMs beat 100 humans without any pixels. Longer reasoning budgets helped. The authors argue this reopens the question of whether a pictorial format is needed.
numbers: Human mean score 2.85 (N=100). o3 3.13 (p=.0067), o3-Pro 3.31 (p<.0001), GPT-5 3.35 (p=.0004), Gemini 3 Pro 3.65 (SD 1.31, p<.0001). o4-mini 2.66 and Claude Opus 4.1 2.65 not different from humans. o3 with GPT-image-1 added: 2.77 (worse than o3 alone). GPT-5 by reasoning effort: high 3.35, medium 2.97, low 2.53, minimal 2.04. Humans said 'I don't know' 54 times, LLMs 0 times. Small negative link between VVIQ and performance.
limits: Text-only task; the authors list three hypotheses (pure propositional, propositional with visual priors, hidden pictorial) and do not separate them. Older or cheaper models scored poorly. Single-lab preprint.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a verbal chain can do tasks said to need images, so a spatial form is not always required. Also: adding generated images hurt o3 here. More reasoning tokens helped, at a cost.

source: Li, Wu, Zhang, Xia, Mao, Dong, Vulic, Wei (2025) Imagine while Reasoning in Space: Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought (MVoT)
finding: A multimodal model (Anole 7B, fine-tuned with a token discrepancy loss) generates an image after each verbal step. On Maze, MiniBehavior and FrozenLake it matches CoT and beats it where CoT breaks.
numbers: MVoT: Maze 92.95%, MiniBehavior 95.14%, FrozenLake 85.60%. Direct prompting about 70%. CoT over 95% on Maze and MiniBehavior (only when the layout is given as text coordinates) but below Direct on FrozenLake; 90.80% of CoT FrozenLake errors came from wrong hole coordinates; CoT fell from 0.9401 (3x3) to 0.3911 (6x6) while MVoT stayed above 83%. Adding MVoT visual thoughts to GPT-4o gave over +15 points on all tasks. Upper bound of MVoT/CoT mixture near 100% on Maze and MiniBehavior, 92% on FrozenLake.
limits: Fine-tuned small model on synthetic grid tasks. CoT without a text layout underperforms Direct. Image generation quality is a cost (blur, redundancy).
agent_relevance: Where coordinate descriptions get long and error-prone, a pictured state is more robust than a written one. Suggests offering a rendered grid check when entity count grows.

source: Zeller, Wiedemer, Li, Klein, Mayilvahanan, Bethge, Wichmann, Cotterell, Brendel (2026) MentisOculi: Revealing the Limits of Reasoning with Mental Imagery
finding: Five procedural multi-step tasks (Form Board, Hinge Folding, Paper Fold, Rush Hour, Sliding Puzzle) at five difficulty levels. Visual strategies from latent tokens to generated images mostly fail to improve accuracy. Unified models can solve the text version, can sometimes draw correct states, but suffer compounding drawing errors and cannot use even ground-truth visuals well.
numbers: At Level 5 all models are at or below chance, some below. Gemini 3 and GPT-5.1 reach human level on the text Rush Hour. Video models (Veo 3.1, Wan 2.6) never exceed chance. Oracle visuals help Gemini on Form Board but not on Hinge Folding or Paper Fold. More thinking tokens did not raise accuracy.
quote: visual thoughts do not yet benefit model reasoning
limits: Specific tasks and models; exact per-cell accuracies not extracted. Results may change with better unified models.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to VoT. Do not assume pictures help. Per G7, require a measured win at equal tokens before keeping a visual form.

source: Hayashi & Hirata (2026) Limits of Spatial Imagery Reasoning in Frontier LLM Models
finding: An MLLM was given an external imagery module that renders and rotates 3D models, to take the load of mental rotation. It still failed. The authors say the models lack depth sensitivity, motion sensitivity, short-horizon dynamic prediction, and the ability to shift visual focus while mixing imagery with symbolic information.
numbers: Best accuracy 62.5% (range 50% to 62.5% over 10 runs); one image-matching test 52.5%; no variation broke the 62.5% ceiling. A pose-recovery test reached 51.25% and one test 17.5%. Reported human-versus-model gap of more than 45% on a cited benchmark.
limits: One architecture and small item counts. Text extraction of the paper was partly binary, so some table values were not read.
agent_relevance: Offloading the transformation to a tool does not fix the reader. In our scaffold, the check of spatial results should be computed by code, not read off a picture by the model.

source: Cooper & Shepard (1973) Chronometric studies of the rotation of mental images (as summarised in Wikipedia, a04)
finding: Reaction times for judging rotated letters rose with rotation angle up to 180 deg and returned to baseline at 360 deg, which fits a mental-rotation reading better than a lookup of stored views.
numbers: Peak at 180 deg, baseline at 360 deg (as stated on the Wikipedia page; the original paper was not opened).
limits: Secondary source only. Later work shows practice with a stimulus reduces the slope, which bounds the effect.
agent_relevance: Shows the cost curve is a signature to measure. Tokens used by a spatial step versus transformation size is the analogous check for an agent.

source: Pylyshyn (2003) Return of the mental image: are there really pictures in the brain? Trends Cogn Sci 7:113-118
finding: Short reply to Kosslyn, Ganis & Thompson (2003, 'against the nihilistic hypothesis'). Argues that retinotopic activation in imagery does not show a pictorial representation, since patterns of activity are not pictures to be read by anyone.
numbers: None (argument paper; not opened). Existence confirmed through Europe PMC listing, not the text.
limits: Not opened. Kosslyn replies that the debate is empirical, not nihilistic.
agent_relevance: Reminds us that 'a spatial pattern is present' does not mean 'a spatial pattern is used'. For the agent, ablate the grid to see if the answer needs it.

source: Kosslyn, Thompson, Kim & Alpert (1995) Topographical representations of mental images in primary visual cortex, Nature 378:496-498
finding: PET study: imagining pictures at small size activated posterior V1, large size anterior V1, as for real viewing. Taken as evidence that imagery uses a topographic map.
numbers: Few subjects (about 8, recalled; not read).
limits: Not opened. Pearson et al. (a13) note that about 20 imaging studies split on V1 activation; Bridge (a14) shows imagery without V1.
agent_relevance: The best-known brain argument for a depictive format; replicated unevenly. Treat as supporting, not proof.
